description: From the theremin to the clubs of Chicago and Detroit, electronic music invents sounds without an orchestra and changes the way the world dances.

hero.hook: From laboratories to dancefloors: how machines invented a new kind of music.

blocks.text: Electronic music did not start in a nightclub. It was born in laboratories, when inventors went looking for sounds no violin or piano could produce.

From the [[Theremin]] of the 1920s to [[Chicago house]] and [[Detroit techno]], one idea runs through the century: a machine can create, not only record. Today it shapes a huge share of global pop and of the [[charts]].

In **1920**, the Russian inventor **Leon Theremin** (Lev Termen) designed the [[Theremin]], an instrument played without being touched. The hands move near two antennas inside an electromagnetic field. The sound slides, almost like a voice, and it soon haunted science fiction films.

blocks.caption: The theremin: an instrument played in the air, without touching a string

blocks.text: After 1945, the research moved to new ground. In Paris, at the public radio, **Pierre Schaeffer** and **Pierre Henry** invented musique concrète: record everyday noises, then cut them, reverse them, loop them on magnetic tape. In Cologne, other studios preferred pure synthesis, sounds born from oscillators with no acoustic source. Those two paths still underpin the way music is made today: [[sampling]] on one side, synthesis on the other.
Theremin showed his instrument to Lenin. The Soviet leader was fascinated and is said to have ordered hundreds of them to spread technical modernity across the USSR.

sections.title: The pioneers: from the theremin to musique concrète

blocks.text: In the 1960s, the American engineer **Robert Moog** shrank the synthesizer with transistors. In **1968**, the album *Switched-On Bach* by **Wendy Carlos** proved that electronics could carry classical complexity. The gadget became an instrument.

blocks.caption: The Moog synthesizer: the machine leaves the lab for the studio

blocks.text: In Düsseldorf, the German band **Kraftwerk**, founded by **Ralf Hütter** and **Florian Schneider**, imposed a cold, repetitive kind of pop. With *Autobahn* (**1974**) and *The Man-Machine* (**1978**), they sang about the highway, the robot, the city. Their beat would later feed American hip-hop and European dance music.

blocks.caption: Kraftwerk: the man-machine as an artistic persona

blocks.text: On some tours, Kraftwerk sent mannequins of themselves to press conferences, pushing the man-machine idea as far as it could go.

sections.title: The Moog, Wendy Carlos and Kraftwerk

blocks.text: In the 1980s, affordable machines like the **Roland TR-808** drum machine changed everything. In Chicago, in clubs filled with Black and gay crowds, the DJ **Frankie Knuckles** refined [[Chicago house]]: a steady 4/4 beat and a warmth inherited from disco.

In **Detroit**, a city hollowed out by the decline of the car factories, three college friends (**Juan Atkins**, **Derrick May**, **Kevin Saunderson**) invented a darker sound: [[Detroit techno]]. Exported to Europe, it found a strong echo in Berlin after the fall of the Wall.
The TR-808 was a commercial flop: professionals called it “unrealistic”. Sold off cheap secondhand, it became the weapon of Chicago's broke DJs.

sections.title: Chicago and Detroit: electronic dance music

blocks.text: From the 1990s on, [[DAW software]] (computer-assisted music) turned an ordinary PC into a studio. Electronics left the club for advertising, film and almost all of pop. [[Chicago house and Detroit techno]] remain the roots of a global language.
